HSTU’s original paper establishes an architecture for nonstationary recommendation streams, but its performance results do not establish sensitivity to specific recent events or higher-order ordering ([Zhai et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152)). Controlled shuffling has direct precedent: a RecSys 2024 study found weak sequential structure in several popular datasets ([Does It Look Sequential?](https://publications.hse.ru/en/chapters/984043670)). A 2025 follow-up distinguishes user-order patterns from item availability through constrained shuffling, warning that apparent temporal structure can reflect when items enter the catalog ([Disentangling User and Item Sequence Patterns](https://researchportal.helsinki.fi/en/publications/disentangling-user-and-item-sequence-patterns-in-sequential-recom/)).

Recency deserves separate measurement: a 2024 workshop paper reports that excessive recency bias can impair recommendation accuracy ([Oh and Cho](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722)). A 2026 study also finds strong recency-weighted pairwise probes competitive with Transformer recommenders on several benchmarks, questioning whether those benchmarks require higher-order modeling ([Petrov et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833)). These findings motivate diagnostics; they do not establish the behavior of this HSTU checkpoint.

Suggested ModelView probe: hold the trained model and validation candidates fixed; compare recent-event deletion, older-history truncation, and valid-event shuffling against equal-count random deletion. Include shuffling that preserves the final event to distinguish broader ordering from last-item dependence. Repack retained events with left padding and read the final nonpadding position. Report paired target-rank changes, HR@10 changes, and top-10 overlap, stratified by category, history length, and observed time gaps. Keep catalog eligibility and seen-item filtering fixed across interventions. Interpret differences as model sensitivity under altered inputs, potentially including distribution shift—not causal evidence of user preferences.
